newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Miners reach end of tether in Russian Far East.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Miners reach end of tether in Russian Far East.

text.p: Tears welling up in his eyes, Pavel Makarkin gives full vent to his frustration.
"You cannot imagine how hard this is, and how humiliating. To have no money to buy your children clothes and schoolbooks, to have to live off your elderly parents' pensions," he said.
Makarkin, like most miners in Russia's Far East region of Primorsky Krai, has not been paid in half a year.
He grows vegetables on his small allotment and engages in barter. His wife, who works in a local hospital, has also not been paid for months.
Some of his workmates at the Amurskaya mine have started donating blood just to make a bit of cash.

This week, their stoicism finally nearing its limits, miners' unions in this rugged, remote region that borders the Pacific Ocean said they had stopped all coal deliveries to power stations until their wages were paid.
But the men are still digging for coal. They fear that an all-out strike would mean the permanent closure of their pit and loss of their livelihood.
MINERS JUST ONE OF MANY GROUPS CAUGHT IN VICIOUS TRAP
"If we stopped working completely, the mine could close for good," said Yury Sherbanyuk, chief engineer at the mine, which is just outside the strategic port city of Vladivostok.
He said miners in the region were now owed as much as seven billion roubles ($1.2 million) in unpaid salaries.
The miners are just one link in a long chain of debt binding customers and suppliers, private and state firms, local and central government.
Many social groups across the vast Russian Federation, including pensioners, teachers and doctors, have been caught up in the same web of delayed payments.
But the miners' latest protests have brought into sharper focus the Russian Far East's acute energy crisis, which has been brewing for several years.
"Power cuts, living by candle-light, cooking on kerosene stoves -- this has been our reality for three years now," said Yelena, one typically frustrated housewife.
TENSIONS RISE AS ENERGY CRISIS BITES
But things have been getting decidely worse of late.
Last week the municipal authorities declared a state of emergency in Vladivostok, a city of 700,000 people, to help ensure regular power supplies to hospitals and other providers of vital services.

Angry crowds have resorted to blocking traffic in certain areas particularly badly affected by the power cuts. Envy has led some citizens to try to sabotage electricity supplies to better-connected neighbourhoods.

Traffic police now have to spend a lot more time directing the cars and trucks -- most of them imported, right-hand drive vehicles imported from nearby Japan -- negotiating the city's pot-holed streets due to malfunctioning traffic lights.
After receiving threatening phone calls, the chiefs of the regional power utility, Dalenergo, have been given special police protection.

Many locals, including the miners, regard Dalenergo as the main culprit behind Vladivostok's energy crisis, but the utility, also caught up in the non-payments web, says it is owed more than two trillion roubles ($348 million) by customers, including the municipal authorities.
POLITICAL NEGLECT FUELS CRISIS
Ageing power stations, a lopsided pricing system and Dalenergo's Soviet-style monopoly on the energy sector have all been cited as factors contributing to Primorsky Krai's plight.

Vladivostok, a closed city until a few years ago, has also inherited from the Soviet era a huge expensive military-industrial complex that consumes a lot of energy without having the ability to pay for it.

But experts say the resource-rich Russian Far East, whose economic potential in the dynamic Pacific Rim region remains largely untapped, has also suffered from mismanagement and lack of strategic planning.

"The regional government should have acted years ago to forestall this crisis by investing in the energy sector with the help of international loans," said one foreign banker, who asked not to be named.
"St Petersburg also inherited a big military-industrial complex from communist days but its leaders planned ahead, they invested in the power sector," the banker added.
The local politicians often seem more interested in trading insults than pooling efforts to resolve the crisis.
REGION LOOKS TO MOSCOW TO RESOLVE IMPASSE
Mayor Viktor Cherepkov accuses regional governor Yevgeny Nazdratenko of helping engineer the power shortages by refusing to allow higher electricity tariffs.
Nazdratenko, a robust populist, says that will lead to industrial collapse.

Now Vladivostok, so eager to hook its destiny to its wealthy neighbours Japan and South Korea, is having to turn back to its traditional paymaster, Moscow, which lies seven time zones and 7,000 km (4,500 miles) to the west.

Cherepkov has gone to the capital to seek the backing of the powerful liberals in broad control of Russian economic policy -- Finance Minister Anatoly Chubais and Energy and Fuel Minister Boris Nemtsov, both first deputy premiers in President Boris Yeltsin's recently revamped Kremlin team.

Vladivostok's Deputy Mayor Yury Kopylov, head of the city's civic emergency committee, told reporters on Wednesday that Cherepkov wanted to canvas support for creating an energy system independent of Dalenergo's control.

But as the politicians vie for influence in the corridors of power, the miners back at Amurskaya colliery -- whose entrance still sports a now painfully ironic Soviet-era slogan "Glory of the Miner" -- have more immediate concerns.
"I'm off to tend my vegetable patch. I hate to think where the family would be without it," said Makarkin.
With a fatalistic sigh, he added: "This is a rich country, the richest in the world in fact. So why can't they pay us?"
